Hey Alex —

Thanks for the clear questions. Short answers up front, then some implementation notes and a small SDK example below. Happy to run through line-by-line in the deep-dive.

Short answers
- Vector dim: We recommend 1536 for modern open embeddings (best tradeoff for semantic retrieval quality). Options: 
  - Re-embed everything to 1536 for a single consistent index (recommended if you can tolerate backfill cost).
  - Keep 1024 historical vectors and run dual-index (or store both dims) + hybrid retrieval. This avoids full re-embed but adds complexity to scoring and storage.
  - If you need a quick migration, do incremental re-embed by priority (hot docs first), keep old index for cold reads.
- Latency/cost delta: 1536 vectors are ~1.5x the bytes vs 1024 — network + storage grows roughly linearly; GPU inference token costs are unaffected since embeddings cost is dominated by model compute. Retrieval latency difference is typically small if your ANN index is tuned, but memory/IO increases. We included a sizing table (attached) with estimated costs for 10M / 50M vector sets.
- Batching: For offline backfill we recommend batching 1k-10k depending on your job parallelism; for online writes use 64-256 per request to balance latency and throughput. Our hosted embedding endpoint supports async bulk writes that accept up to ~2k vectors per request (we can adjust for enterprise plans).
- Normalization: For cosine similarity, normalize vectors to unit length (L2) and use dot-product for fast ANN indexes. Redwood has a normalization flag in the SDK (normalize=true) which stores normalized vectors if you select cosine mode. If you plan to mix dot and cosine, keep normalized unit vectors to keep scoring consistent.
- Reranker: Typical pattern — ANN candidate retrieval (top 100) -> fast logits-based reranker or cross-encoder on top 10-20. To minimize reranker calls: increase candidate quality with dense+BM25 hybrid retrieval, cap reranker to top-K (10-20), and cache reranker results for common queries.

Implementation notes
- Migration strategy (recommended)
 1) Snapshot current index + export metadata 
 2) Prioritize hot sets (top-traffic docs) and backfill in waves (parallel workers) using batch size ~512. 
 3) Run shadow traffic: route a % of search requests to new index and compare recall/latency. 
 4) Once validated, switch traffic and retire old index.

- SDK & auth
We support API keys and service-account style tokens. For automation you should create a service account with limited scope (embeddings:write, embeddings:read, index:manage) and rotate keys via your secrets manager. Example (Python, simplified):

from redwood import RedwoodClient
client = RedwoodClient(api_key="REDACTED")
# batch example
texts = ["doc1 text...", "doc2 text..."]
resp = client.embeddings.create(model="text-embed-1536", input=texts, batch_size=128, normalize=True)
# resp will contain a list of vectors (one per input)

- Routing & regions
You can pin requests to a region (us-east/us-west/eu) via the SDK config. Redwood also supports policy-based routing if you want cheaper model variants to handle lower-priority queries.
